primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Increasing pulsatile hypothalamic GnRH secretion stimulates pituitary LH and FSH release and activates gonadal steroid production during puberty.
vignette: A healthy 11-year-old girl begins breast development followed several months later by a rapid increase in height. She has no chronic illness and takes no medications.
lead: Which physiologic change most directly initiates normal activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis at puberty?
correct: Increased pulsatile secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone
distractors: Continuous nonpulsatile secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone
Decreased pituitary responsiveness to gonadotropin-releasing hormone
Suppression of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone secretion
Primary loss of ovarian estrogen synthesis
distractor_notes: Continuous GnRH exposure downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors and suppresses gonadotropin release rather than initiating normal puberty.
Pituitary responsiveness is not normally reduced at pubertal onset; the axis becomes functionally activated.
LH and FSH rise during normal puberty and stimulate gonadal steroidogenesis rather than being suppressed.
Normal puberty reflects activation of an intact gonadal axis, not primary ovarian failure.
key_expl: Normal puberty begins with reactivation of pulsatile hypothalamic GnRH secretion, which drives pituitary LH/FSH release and gonadal sex-steroid production.
objective: Recognize pulsatile GnRH secretion as the central physiologic trigger for activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis at puberty.

sources.title: Puberty
sources.locator: Overview of normal pubertal hormonal and physical changes
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes puberty as a hormonally driven period in which the body becomes sexually mature.

sources.title: Puberty and Precocious Puberty
sources.support: NICHD describes activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and gonadotropin-driven gonadal maturation during puberty.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Deoxygenated hemoglobin S polymerizes because a beta-globin glutamate-to-valine substitution creates a hydrophobic interaction, deforming erythrocytes and promoting vaso-occlusion.
vignette: A 14-year-old boy with sickle cell disease develops severe pain in both legs after prolonged exercise and dehydration. Peripheral blood smear shows sickled erythrocytes.
lead: Which molecular event most directly causes the acute erythrocyte deformation in this patient?
distractors: Oxidation of hemoglobin after impaired NADPH generation
Defective heme synthesis from iron and protoporphyrin
distractor_notes: Alpha-globin synthesis defects cause alpha-thalassemia and do not produce HbS polymer formation.
Spectrin or anchoring-protein defects cause membrane instability and spherocytosis rather than sickling.
Impaired NADPH production characterizes G6PD deficiency and causes oxidant hemolysis rather than HbS polymerization.
Defective heme synthesis causes sideroblastic or related anemias and does not explain deoxygenation-triggered sickling.
key_expl: HbS polymerizes when deoxygenated; the resulting rigid fibers distort erythrocytes and promote vaso-occlusion.
objective: Link the beta-globin substitution in sickle cell disease to deoxygenation-dependent HbS polymerization and erythrocyte sickling.

sources.title: Sickle cell disease
sources.locator: Causes; molecular effect of hemoglobin S
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics explains that HBB variants produce hemoglobin S, which can form rigid structures that distort red blood cells.

sources.title: HBB gene
sources.locator: Normal Function; Health Conditions Related to Genetic Changes
sources.support: The HBB gene encodes beta-globin; the sickle variant alters beta-globin and causes hemoglobin molecules to assemble abnormally.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: G6PD deficiency lowers pentose-phosphate-pathway NADPH generation, impairing maintenance of reduced glutathione and increasing erythrocyte susceptibility to oxidative injury.
vignette: A 22-year-old man develops jaundice and dark urine 2 days after receiving an oxidant medication. Blood smear shows bite cells and Heinz-body-associated damage.
lead: Deficiency of which metabolic product most directly increases this patient's erythrocyte susceptibility to oxidative stress?
distractor_notes: FADH2 is generated in oxidative metabolism, but mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and oxidant protection depends on NADPH.
Acetyl-CoA is central to intermediary metabolism but is not the reducing equivalent used to regenerate reduced glutathione in erythrocytes.
cAMP is a signaling second messenger and does not provide reducing power for glutathione recycling.
UDP-glucose participates in glycogen and carbohydrate metabolism and does not protect erythrocytes from oxidant injury.
key_expl: G6PD is the rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway in erythrocytes; the pathway generates NADPH needed to keep glutathione reduced.
objective: Explain oxidant-triggered hemolysis in G6PD deficiency through deficient NADPH generation and impaired glutathione reduction.

sources.title: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics explains that reduced G6PD activity makes red blood cells vulnerable to oxidative damage and hemolysis.

sources.title: G6PD gene
sources.support: G6PD participates in the pentose phosphate pathway and helps protect red blood cells from reactive oxygen species.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Defects in erythrocyte membrane-cytoskeletal proteins reduce membrane stability and surface area, producing poorly deformable spherocytes that are trapped and destroyed in the spleen.
vignette: A 12-year-old boy has chronic mild jaundice, splenomegaly, and anemia. His father underwent splenectomy for a similar disorder. Peripheral smear shows numerous spherocytes.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains this patient's findings?
distractors: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia due to a transient drug exposure
distractor_notes: G6PD deficiency typically causes episodic oxidant-triggered hemolysis with bite cells or Heinz-body injury rather than a familial chronic spherocytic anemia.
Sickle cell disease produces sickled cells and vaso-occlusive manifestations rather than isolated familial spherocytosis.
Beta-thalassemia major causes severe microcytic anemia with globin-chain imbalance and characteristic target cells, not this dominant familial pattern.
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia can produce spherocytes, but the lifelong familial pattern strongly favors an inherited membrane disorder.
key_expl: A dominant family history, chronic extravascular hemolysis, splenomegaly, and spherocytes are classic for hereditary spherocytosis.
objective: Recognize hereditary spherocytosis from chronic familial extravascular hemolysis with spherocytes and splenomegaly.

sources.title: Hereditary spherocytosis
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes hereditary spherocytosis as an inherited red-cell membrane disorder causing spherical cells, anemia, jaundice, and splenomegaly.

sources.title: ANK1 gene
sources.support: ANK1 encodes ankyrin, which helps attach the erythrocyte membrane to its cytoskeleton; pathogenic variants can cause hereditary spherocytosis.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Quantitative or qualitative deficiency of von Willebrand factor impairs platelet adhesion and reduces stabilization of coagulation factor VIII.
vignette: A 19-year-old woman has recurrent epistaxis, easy bruising, and prolonged bleeding after dental procedures. Her mother has similar symptoms. Platelet count is normal.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains this pattern of bleeding?
distractor_notes: Hemophilia A usually causes deep tissue and joint bleeding and follows X-linked inheritance rather than autosomal mucocutaneous bleeding in women.
Immune thrombocytopenia causes a low platelet count, which is absent here.
Disseminated intravascular coagulation occurs in severely ill patients with systemic coagulation activation and consumption, not a lifelong familial mucosal bleeding pattern.
Factor V Leiden increases venous thrombosis risk rather than causing mucocutaneous bleeding.
key_expl: Inherited mucocutaneous bleeding with normal platelet count is characteristic of von Willebrand disease, the most common inherited bleeding disorder.
objective: Differentiate von Willebrand disease from coagulation-factor deficiencies and platelet-count disorders using the pattern of mucocutaneous bleeding.
clues: autosomal family history with normal platelet count

sources.title: Von Willebrand disease
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes von Willebrand disease as an inherited bleeding disorder caused by deficient or dysfunctional von Willebrand factor.

sources.title: VWF gene
sources.support: VWF encodes von Willebrand factor, which participates in platelet adhesion and carries/stabilizes factor VIII.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Factor VIII deficiency impairs the intrinsic tenase complex, reducing activation of factor X and thrombin generation during secondary hemostasis.
vignette: An 8-year-old boy has recurrent hemarthroses after minor trauma. His maternal uncle had similar episodes. Platelet count and prothrombin time are normal, and activated partial thromboplastin time is prolonged.
lead: Which coagulation protein is most likely deficient?
distractor_notes: Von Willebrand factor deficiency usually causes mucocutaneous bleeding and may secondarily reduce factor VIII, but recurrent hemarthroses with X-linked inheritance is classic hemophilia A.
Factor VII deficiency primarily prolongs the extrinsic pathway and prothrombin time rather than isolated aPTT.
Factor XIII deficiency does not prolong routine PT or aPTT because it acts after fibrin formation.
Protein C deficiency predisposes to thrombosis, not recurrent hemarthroses.
key_expl: Hemophilia A is an X-linked factor VIII deficiency causing impaired intrinsic-pathway coagulation and deep tissue or joint bleeding.
objective: Relate recurrent hemarthroses, X-linked inheritance, and prolonged aPTT to factor VIII deficiency in hemophilia A.
clues: maternal male relative with normal PT and prolonged aPTT

sources.title: Hemophilia
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes hemophilia A as factor VIII deficiency causing prolonged bleeding and joint hemorrhage.

sources.title: F8 gene
sources.support: F8 encodes coagulation factor VIII, a cofactor required for efficient activation of factor X in the intrinsic pathway.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Iron depletion limits heme synthesis, producing progressively microcytic hypochromic erythrocytes with low ferritin and increased iron-binding capacity.
vignette: A 32-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding has fatigue and pica. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume is 70 fL, serum ferritin is low, and total iron-binding capacity is elevated.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains these findings?
distractor_notes: Beta-thalassemia trait can be microcytic but typically has normal or increased iron stores and does not cause low ferritin from chronic blood loss.
Anemia of chronic inflammation usually features normal or increased ferritin with reduced total iron-binding capacity.
Vitamin B12 deficiency produces macrocytosis rather than microcytosis.
Hereditary spherocytosis produces hemolytic anemia with spherocytes rather than low iron stores and pica.
key_expl: Chronic menstrual blood loss, pica, microcytosis, low ferritin, and elevated iron-binding capacity establish iron deficiency anemia.
objective: Diagnose iron deficiency anemia from characteristic clinical risk factors and iron studies.
clues: heavy menstrual blood loss and pica

sources.title: Iron deficiency anemia
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes chronic blood loss as a common cause of iron deficiency anemia and notes characteristic low iron stores.

sources.title: Iron — Health Professional Fact Sheet
sources.support: NIH ODS describes iron deficiency as limiting hemoglobin production and causing microcytic anemia when severe.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Vitamin B12 deficiency impairs methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase reactions, producing defective DNA synthesis and accumulation of methylmalonic acid with neurologic injury.
vignette: A 66-year-old man has fatigue, paresthesias, and impaired vibration sense. Laboratory studies show macrocytic anemia and hypersegmented neutrophils.
lead: Which metabolite is most likely elevated because of this vitamin deficiency?
distractor_notes: Homogentisic acid accumulates in alkaptonuria, not vitamin B12 deficiency.
Phenylalanine accumulates in phenylketonuria.
Galactose-1-phosphate accumulates in classic galactosemia.
Branched-chain alpha-ketoacids accumulate in maple syrup urine disease.
key_expl: Vitamin B12 is required for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; deficiency therefore raises methylmalonic acid and can produce neurologic deficits.
objective: Distinguish vitamin B12 deficiency biochemically by elevated methylmalonic acid in a patient with macrocytic anemia and neurologic findings.
clues: paresthesias and loss of vibration sense

sources.title: Vitamin B12 — Health Professional Fact Sheet
sources.support: NIH ODS describes vitamin B12 as a cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and notes neurologic manifestations of deficiency.

sources.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes megaloblastic anemia and neurologic manifestations associated with vitamin B12 deficiency.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Defective phagocyte NADPH oxidase prevents an effective respiratory burst and superoxide generation, impairing intracellular killing of selected bacteria and fungi.
vignette: A 6-year-old boy has recurrent deep abscesses caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus species. Dihydrorhodamine testing shows minimal fluorescence after neutrophil stimulation.
lead: Which cellular function is most directly impaired?
correct: Generation of superoxide by NADPH oxidase
distractors: Production of immunoglobulin by plasma cells
Expression of beta-2 integrins on neutrophils
distractor_notes: Phagolysosomal fusion defects cause different intracellular-killing disorders and are not identified by an abnormal oxidative-burst assay.
Antibody-production failure causes humoral immunodeficiency rather than an abnormal neutrophil oxidative burst.
Beta-2 integrin deficiency causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency with impaired tissue migration, delayed cord separation, and little pus.
Membrane attack complexes are generated by complement and are not measured by neutrophil dihydrorhodamine testing.
key_expl: The dihydrorhodamine assay measures the oxidative burst; chronic granulomatous disease reflects deficient NADPH oxidase and impaired superoxide production.
objective: Connect an abnormal dihydrorhodamine oxidative-burst test with NADPH oxidase deficiency in chronic granulomatous disease.

sources.title: Chronic granulomatous disease
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics explains that CGD impairs phagocyte production of reactive oxygen species needed to kill microbes.

sources.title: CYBB gene
sources.support: CYBB encodes a component of NADPH oxidase required for the phagocyte respiratory burst.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: BTK deficiency arrests B-cell maturation at the pre-B-cell stage, causing markedly reduced mature B cells and all immunoglobulin classes after maternal IgG wanes.
vignette: An 11-month-old boy has recurrent otitis media and pneumonia beginning at 7 months of age. Tonsils are very small. Laboratory studies show nearly absent circulating B cells and markedly reduced concentrations of all immunoglobulin classes.
correct: Maturation of pre-B cells into mature B lymphocytes
distractors: Positive selection of T lymphocytes in the thymus
Class switching in already mature plasma cells only
distractor_notes: Defective thymic T-cell selection causes cellular immunodeficiency rather than selective absence of mature B cells.
Defective neutrophil superoxide generation causes chronic granulomatous disease, not agammaglobulinemia.
The defect occurs before mature B-cell formation, so it is not merely an isolated class-switching problem.
Terminal complement deficiency predisposes particularly to Neisseria infections but does not eliminate circulating B cells and immunoglobulins.
key_expl: BTK signaling is required for B-cell maturation; loss of BTK blocks development before mature B lymphocytes form.
objective: Explain the absent B cells and pan-hypogammaglobulinemia of X-linked agammaglobulinemia as a pre-B-cell maturation defect.
clues: infections beginning after maternal antibody wanes
absent B cells and very small tonsils

sources.title: X-linked agammaglobulinemia
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes XLA as a BTK-related block in B-cell development causing very low mature B cells and immunoglobulins.

sources.title: BTK gene
sources.support: BTK encodes a signaling protein required for normal B-cell development and maturation.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Adenosine deaminase deficiency severe combined immunodeficiency
mechanism: ADA deficiency causes accumulation of toxic purine metabolites, including deoxyadenosine-derived nucleotides, which are particularly toxic to developing lymphocytes and cause severe combined immunodeficiency.
vignette: A 4-month-old infant has persistent oral candidiasis, recurrent pneumonia, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive. Lymphocyte count is profoundly decreased, and testing shows adenosine deaminase deficiency.
lead: Accumulation of which substrate most directly contributes to lymphocyte toxicity?
distractor_notes: Homogentisic acid accumulates in alkaptonuria and causes ochronosis.
Fructose-1-phosphate accumulates in hereditary fructose intolerance.
GM2 ganglioside accumulates in Tay-Sachs disease.
Glucocerebroside accumulates in Gaucher disease.
key_expl: ADA normally participates in purine metabolism; its deficiency permits deoxyadenosine-derived metabolites to accumulate and damage lymphocytes.
objective: Relate ADA deficiency to toxic purine-metabolite accumulation and combined T- and B-cell immunodeficiency.

sources.title: Adenosine deaminase deficiency
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics explains that ADA deficiency causes toxic purine metabolites to accumulate and destroy lymphocytes, producing SCID.

sources.title: ADA gene
sources.support: ADA encodes adenosine deaminase, which is required for normal purine metabolism and lymphocyte survival.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Deletion or inactivation of alpha-globin genes reduces alpha-chain production, causing excess beta-like chains and severity proportional to the number of affected alpha-globin alleles.
vignette: A newborn is found to have microcytosis. Genetic testing shows deletion of three alpha-globin genes.
lead: Which abnormal hemoglobin is most likely to be prominent after birth in this patient?
distractors: Gamma-globin tetramers as the only persistent abnormal hemoglobin
Normal adult hemoglobin with no chain imbalance
distractor_notes: Alpha-globin tetramers cannot form when alpha-chain production is deficient.
Gamma tetramers can form prenatally as hemoglobin Bart's, but after birth beta-chain tetramers form hemoglobin H in three-gene deletion disease.
Three-gene alpha-globin deletion creates substantial chain imbalance and does not yield only normal adult hemoglobin.
Hemoglobin S polymers result from a structural beta-globin variant rather than alpha-globin gene deletion.
key_expl: Loss of three alpha-globin genes causes hemoglobin H disease; after birth, excess beta chains form beta4 tetramers called hemoglobin H.
objective: Relate the number of deleted alpha-globin genes to hemoglobin H formation in alpha-thalassemia.

sources.title: Alpha thalassemia
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes alpha-thalassemia severity according to the number of affected alpha-globin genes and identifies hemoglobin H disease with three-gene loss.

sources.title: HBA1 gene
sources.support: HBA1 contributes alpha-globin chains to hemoglobin; reduced alpha-globin production creates globin-chain imbalance.
